\section{Actuarial impact}
\label{sec:actuarial}

\noindent\textit{The shift column of Table~\ref{tab:h5-actuarial} is final:
it is generated from the QA-passed shift results files and every shift
number quoted below is read from that fragment. The stable and placebo
columns are pending---no results file for either regime has passed the QA
gate---and no stable- or placebo-derived statement is made in this
section.}

\subsection{H5: propagation into life expectancy and annuity factors}

% tab-h5-actuarial is a page-spanning longtable fragment generated by
% scripts/make_tables.py; it carries its own \caption and \label{tab:h5-actuarial}.
\inputtable{tab-h5-actuarial}

Table~\ref{tab:h5-actuarial} reports, for each family--mechanism cell and
regime, the empirical coverage of the central 95\% interval and the mean
error for period life expectancy at birth and at 65 and for the annuity-due
factor at 65 and 2\%, each computed on the period table of the first test
year from the cell's own sample paths and compared with the same functional
of the observed rates. The functionals are taken from the latent rate paths
of every distributional cell, before the Poisson composition that the
rate-scale scores use. Three conventions of the table govern its reading.
Conformal cells have no such paths---their samples are uniform draws inside
a band, a convention for interval metrics only---so their derived-quantity
rows are not applicable and the table marks them \emph{n/a} rather than
tabulating a distributional claim. CBD is fit on ages 55--99: it
contributes no $e_0$, and its $e_{65}$ and $\annuity$ are exact on the
truncated 55--99 table, so its rows are not on the same footing as the
full-age families'. And the sparse VAR, multi-output GP and LSTM rows carry
fewer than the forty (population, sex, origin) units of the shift design
because their error rows (Table~\ref{tab:infeasible}) are excluded from
every mean; $n$ and $n_{\mathrm{err}}$ are tabulated per cell. \Hfive\ is
restricted by Addendum~3 (\S8) to the ex-post coverage of these derived
intervals, with the attenuation alternative---that life-table integration
averages a rate-surface failure away \citep{cairns2011mortality}---as the
named competitor. Both outcomes are informative: the first says the
reserve is wrong, the second says the audit's headline is a statement
about rates rather than about liabilities.

\Hfive\ was registered as: \emph{interval miscalibration propagates to
derived quantities---empirical coverage of 95\% intervals for $e_{65}$ and
the annuity factor $\annuity$ at 2\% departs from nominal by more than the
corresponding stable-regime departure}. The registered contrast therefore
needs the stable column, which is pending; what the shift column settles
is the shift half of the comparison, and it settles it in a form that
leaves the verdict depending only on how close to nominal the stable
regime turns out to be.

In the shift regime, no distributional arm attains nominal coverage on any
of the three functionals. Coverage of the nominal 95\% interval for
$e_{65}$ runs from 0.275 (neural-LC ensemble) to 0.925 (CBD with the
Poisson bootstrap); for $\annuity$ from 0.289 (LSTM ensemble) to 0.850
(CBD under either mechanism); for $e_0$ from 0.263 (LSTM ensemble) to
0.875 (NB-head ensemble). Outside CBD's truncated table no arm exceeds
0.750 on either registered functional---the NB head under MC dropout, at
0.750 on both, is the best full-age cell---and the classical full-age
cores sit at 0.425--0.600 on $e_{65}$. In departure-from-nominal terms:
at least 0.200 for every full-age arm on both registered functionals, and
0.025 ($e_{65}$) and 0.100 ($\annuity$) even for CBD on its own 55--99
table. The mean errors are two-sided across families: on $\annuity$ they
run from $-0.45$ annuity units (LSTM ensemble) to $+0.39$ (NB-head
ensemble), and on $e_{65}$ from $-0.68$ years (LSTM ensemble) to $+0.60$
(NB-head ensemble), with half-year misses of $e_{65}$ ordinary among the
full-age families ($-0.57$ for SVD Lee--Carter, $+0.50$ for neural-LC).
CBD is the exception in location as well as coverage: its $e_{65}$ errors
are $-0.01$ and $+0.02$ and its $\annuity$ errors $-0.04$ and $-0.03$, an
order of magnitude smaller than any full-age family's.

The attenuation alternative is answered by reading this table beside
Table~\ref{tab:h2-coverage}: for every distributional arm except CBD,
coverage of the derived quantities lies \emph{below} the same arm's
marginal coverage on log rates. Integration does not average the
shift-regime failure away; it concentrates it. The mechanism is the one
\Hthree\ measures on the horizon axis, here acting on the age axis: a
period functional integrates the whole scored age range of one test year,
so a common-factor miss that leaves many single-age intervals near but
inside their bounds still displaces the functional, and one displaced
functional is one uncovered cell. A derived quantity behaves as a joint
coverage statement across ages, not a marginal one, and the pandemic
year's miss is exactly the common-factor kind. CBD, the one family whose
derived coverage exceeds its rate-scale coverage, is also the one fit and
integrated on ages 55--99 only; whether its behaviour is a property of
the family or of its truncated support is not separable in this design,
and its rows are read with that caveat.

Under the registered wording, then, the shift half of \Hfive\ is
established quantitatively---departures from nominal of at least 0.200 on
both registered functionals for every full-age arm---and the hypothesis is
supported exactly where the stable-regime departure of the same arm comes
in smaller. The stable files do not yet exist, so that per-arm comparison,
and with it the registered verdict on \Hfive, is pending; the placebo
column, whose first-pass file lacks its GP arm and has not passed the
data-quality gate, is pending in the same sense.

\subsection{Reading a coverage shortfall in balance-sheet terms}

For an annuity-due of one per annum at age 65, the interval on $\annuity$
translates directly into an interval on the best-estimate liability of a
unit annuitant. A nominal 95\% interval that covers the realised
$\annuity$ in materially fewer than 95\% of population--sex cells is, in
Solvency~II language, an internal model whose longevity distribution is
too narrow; in the shift column of Table~\ref{tab:h5-actuarial} that is
every distributional arm---0.850 at best, on CBD's truncated table, and at
most 0.750 for any full-age family. The direction of the central miss is
not the single-signed pandemic effect a uniform mortality margin would
absorb: SVD Lee--Carter, CNN-LC and the LSTM sit below the realised
$\annuity$ on average (mean errors $-0.24$ to $-0.45$), understating the
liability implied by the realised 2020 table even in a pandemic year,
while RH, neural-LC and the NB-head ensemble sit above it ($+0.24$ to
$+0.39$). The shortfall of the model's 97.5\% quantile of $\annuity$
below the realised value, where it occurs, is the amount by which the
implied capital at that level is understated; we report this quantity as
a proportion of the central $\annuity$ so that it is portable across
populations and interest-rate assumptions. \todo{compute from the
$\annuity$ point, upper-quantile and realised columns of the results
files; decide whether a worked example on a hypothetical portfolio adds
anything}

\subsection{The longevity tail}

The 99.5\% upper quantile of the predictive distribution of $\annuity$ is
the one-year longevity tail an internal model would carry. The fraction of
cells in which the realised value exceeds the model's own 99.5\% quantile
is the empirical frequency of a nominally once-in-200-year event, and is the
quantity the pandemic years let us observe for the first time. This is
descriptive and not a registered hypothesis. \todo{the runner emits only
the 2.5\% and 97.5\% sample quantiles of the derived quantities; a 99.5\%
column must be added to the runner and the cells re-scored before this
paragraph can be filled}

\subsection{Twin crises in economic terms}

The placebo rows of Table~\ref{tab:h5-actuarial} supply the same
functionals for 1914--1922. A side-by-side of the $e_{65}$ and $\annuity$
interval coverage across the two events asks whether any break-induced
coverage shortfall is of similar economic size at the two breaks a century
apart, or whether the pandemic years are distinctive---or whether neither
event moves the derived intervals off nominal; the comparison is
descriptive, and the
placebo's first test year is 1914, before the influenza wave, which the
reading must respect. The placebo column is pending: the first-pass
placebo results file lacks its GP arm and has not passed the data-quality
gate, and no placebo-derived number appears in this paper until both
exist.
